Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares
I try to erase the memory of the event
I think about why the event has happened to me

Threat.value: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Negative Appraisals.value: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened

issues.item: Triggers: Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
issues.explanation: For chronic physical abuse by a romantic partner, being triggered by male presence and related people is coherent, but explosion/bang sounds points toward combat, accidents, or blast-related trauma and is hard to reconcile as a core trigger here without any matching assault-context cue elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: The rest of the profile reflects fear, avoidance, hypervigilance, fragmented memory, and negative self/world appraisals. Endorsing risky behavior pulls in the opposite direction and is not supported by other selected items; it reads as a different coping/symptom pattern than the otherwise strongly avoidant-threat profile.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: A marked loss of connection to community and culture is not well anchored to the rest of this intimate-partner-violence profile. The other appraisals center on danger, contamination, and shattered beliefs, but nothing else suggests cultural/community rupture, making this item feel clinically disconnected rather than tightly linked to the stated trauma formulation.

vignette:
Eleanor was eighty years old when she finally walked into a therapist's office, though the decision had been forming for months. The door had slammed again-this time at the grocery store, a heavy metal door closing behind a young man who had held it open for her. The sound had sent her heart into her throat, and she had stood frozen in the produce aisle, unable to move until the manager asked if she needed help. She did not need help; she needed the man to step farther away, to stop being so close, to stop being male.

The event that had shattered her life happened more than fifty years ago, but it lived in her body as though it were yesterday. She had been with a man she trusted-a romantic partner, her first serious relationship after leaving her parents' home. He had come home angry, and she could still see the door frame splintering as he slammed the kitchen door, the noise splitting the quiet evening. She remembered his hand, the way it looked raised in the air, but she could not remember what came before or after. The memory came as snapshots: his knuckles white, the door handle gouging the wall, the feeling of her back against the counter. She could not order them. She could not make them into a story. When the snapshots surfaced, she felt an overwhelming grief that left her breathless, a sorrow not just for herself but for the person she had believed she was.

For decades, Eleanor tried to erase the memory. She would catch herself mentally shoving the images into a box, slamming a lid down, and then forcing herself to think about her case files, her clients, anything else. She avoided the hours of night when dreams were most vivid, staying up until two or three in the morning until exhaustion finally pulled her under, and even then she often lay awake, watching the shadows on the ceiling. Sleep had become a battleground. When she did drift off, the snapshots would replay, jumbled and relentless.

Being a social worker had once been her identity, but over the years she found herself shrinking. She began scheduling home visits only in the mornings, when she could plan an escape route before entering a client's building. She scanned every room for exits-not as a professional assessment, but as a reflex, her eyes darting to doors and windows before she could help it. She stopped taking male colleagues along on joint visits; being alone in a car with a man, even a trusted coworker, made her skin crawl with a sense of contamination that she could not explain. She began to feel dirty when men stood too close, as though something of the old trauma had seeped into her pores and could not be washed out.

Her belief that people were fundamentally good had been destroyed. She no longer trusted anyone, least of all men she knew personally. Her nephew-her sister's son, a gentle man in his fifties-had once visited, and Eleanor found herself unable to sit in the same room with him. She told her sister she was tired, but the truth was that being alone with any man, even a relative, felt like a threat requiring constant vigilance. She found herself staring at the floor, the walls, anywhere but at his face, and she kept a path to the front door clear at all times.

Why had it happened to her? The question looped through her mind for decades. She had been a good person, a helper, a believer in trust. She had been raised to believe that the world was safe if you made good choices. The abuse had erased that belief utterly. She felt contaminated by her own history, as if the dirt of that night clung to her no matter how many showers she took.

Her life contracted slowly. She retired early from social work because she could no longer tolerate the unpredictability of male presence in the office. She lived alone in a small apartment with a deadbolt and a chain. She stopped accepting dinner invitations from her sister if her brother-in-law would be home. She stopped going to the evening senior center events because doors opened and closed constantly, and each slam sent a jolt through her chest.

What finally brought her to seek help was not a crisis-it was a quiet recognition that at eighty, she was running out of time. She was exhausted from the hypervigilance, from the grief that still welled up when she least expected it, from the endless search for meaning that never ended. She wanted, more than anything, to be able to sit in a room with a door closed and not feel her heart race. She wanted to be able to trust that the next door that opened would not bring a raised hand. She was not sure she could ever fully believe that, but she had come to see that carrying it alone was no longer possible.
